Decision guide

Automation agency pricing: fixed fee or retainer?

A purchasing team can receive a fixed implementation price and a monthly retainer for the same order-entry workflow. The cheaper one depends on how often the source systems change and who handles failed jobs. Ask for two prices for the same twelve months of work.

The cost of a completed job

  1. VolumeCount completed jobs
  2. ExceptionsTime retries and reviews
  3. CostInclude ongoing support

Price the first delivery

Specify the trigger, destination systems, required approvals and the record that counts as a completed order. A fixed fee works best when both parties can test that definition. Ask who pays for changes to field mappings discovered during the pilot and whether the buyer can reject a duplicate or incomplete record.

Work through a retainer example

Suppose the fixed bid is $8,000 plus $300 a month in support. Another agency offers $1,050 a month including setup and two small changes per month. With twelve paid months and identical third-party usage, the fixed option costs $11,600 and the retainer costs $12,600. If the fixed bidder charges an extra $1,500 for required changes covered by the retainer, the comparison becomes $13,100 versus $12,600. These figures illustrate the calculation.

Decide what happens during a failure

Ask the agency to separate response time from recovery time. For a delayed order, identify who pauses retries, who checks for a duplicate and who tells the customer that processing resumed. Include the cost of out-of-hours support only when the workflow actually needs it.

Count each accepted order once

Suppose 1,000 distinct orders arrive in a month. The destination accepts 900 on the first attempt. Retrying the other 100 gets 60 more accepted. Staff review the remaining 40 and correct 30 by hand. At month end, 990 orders meet the acceptance rule, including 30 manual completions. The other 10 are still open. Match each accepted destination record to its source order ID so a duplicate write cannot earn a second completion.

Calculate cost per completed workflow

Using the $1,050 retainer above, suppose the tool charges $0.10 per attempt on top of the retainer. The 1,000 first attempts and 100 retries cost $110. Six minutes of staff time on each of the 40 exceptions comes to four hours. At $45 per hour, that adds $180, including time spent on the 10 open orders. The monthly total is $1,340. Divide by 990 accepted orders for $1.35 per completion. Of those orders, 960 finished without manual correction.

Check the calculation against your pilot

Use the same batch and cutoff for both bids. Match the execution log to the destination records, check metered charges against the invoice, and use the time spent on all exceptions. Include support and the same share of one-time setup for each bid, counting fees already bundled in the quote only once. If the batch yields zero accepted orders, report the spend and zero completions. A unit cost cannot yet be calculated.

Decision table
Contract itemRequest from both agencies
UsageCost per execution, model call and connected tool, at your expected volume.
ChangesA written example of an included change and an example that triggers a new quote.
OperationsAlert destination, support hours, escalation owner and handling of failed runs.
ExitWorkflow export, documentation, account ownership and transition cost.

Illustrative buyer scenario

The fixed fee covers the build. Who pays for exceptions?

A sales operations team receives an attractive fixed quote for routing inbound requests. The agency counts every submitted form as a successful run. The team needs a lead in the correct queue, so it also records duplicates, rejected records and entries that a colleague has to correct by hand.

Give the agency a mixed sample. Ask for the number of completed routes, correction minutes and paid tool calls, including retries. Divide the total operating cost by successful routes, then rerun the comparison using a quieter month.

What to keep

A reconciliation from submitted forms to routed leads, the delivery owner for exceptions and the scope of the support fee.

When to pause

Rework a quote that counts retries as extra successes or excludes manual correction from the buyer’s monthly cost.

Make the decision

Review the last three production changes with your operations lead. Price those actual changes under each proposal. If the cheaper agreement depends on never changing a supplier field or an approval rule, take that assumption back to the agency before you sign.
